issues.legal_issue: A party excluded from a title suit by compromise and later granted final restitution is not constructively bound by the decree in that suit.
material_facts: A compromise provided that the respondent’s name would be expunged from the title suit while the decree otherwise stood.
The respondent obtained restitution of the land, and the restitution proceedings finally determined that she was entitled to it as against the title-suit decree.
The appellant relied on the doctrine of lis pendens to argue that the respondent was bound by the decree because her predecessor had been a party to the title suit.
issues.conclusion: The respondent was not bound by the decree in the title suit and could re-agitate the questions decided there.
issues.legal_principle: Under s. 144 of the Code of Civil Procedure, an application for restitution is an application for execution of a decree; res judicata applies to execution proceedings. The compromise was intended to exclude the respondent from being bound by the decree, actually or constructively. The Court applied Mahijibhai v. Manibhai, [1965] 2 S.C.R. 436.

predicates.title_claim_dispute: A party seeks a declaration of title to property affected by an earlier suit decree.
predicates.party_removed_from_prior_suit_by_comprom: A compromise in the earlier suit provides that the party’s name is to be removed from the array of parties.
predicates.restoration_proceeding_finally_determine: A proceeding seeking restoration of property taken under the earlier decree is finally determined in the party’s favour.
predicates.claimant_not_bound_by_prior_decree: The claimant is not bound by the decree in the earlier suit.

issues.definition: When a title claim follows a compromise removing a party from an earlier suit and a final restoration determination in that party’s favour, the party is not bound by the earlier decree.

issues.legal_issue: A claimed oral gift is not proved when the evidence supporting it is materially inconsistent and relevant available evidence is not produced.
material_facts: The appellant claimed that the deceased had orally gifted her share to him.
The date and scope of the alleged gift differed between the appellant’s testimony and his earlier account in the title-suit proceedings.
The appellant’s mother, who was said to have witnessed the gift and was alive, was not called as a witness.
The appellant gave no satisfactory explanation for how he recalled the date of the alleged gift, and the deceased had been dispossessed of the property before the alleged gift.
issues.conclusion: The appellant failed to prove the alleged oral gift.
issues.legal_principle: The alleged gift had to be proved on the evidence. The Court upheld the High Court’s assessment of the inconsistencies, the absence of a relevant available witness, and the surrounding circumstances.

predicates.oral_gift_claim_in_property_dispute: A claimant relies on an alleged oral gift as the basis of a claim to property.
predicates.gift_account_materially_inconsistent: The claimant gives materially differing accounts of the alleged gift in testimony and earlier proceedings or documents.
predicates.available_supporting_witness_not_examine: A living witness said to have observed the gift is not called to give evidence.
predicates.oral_gift_not_proved: The alleged oral gift is not established by the evidence.

issues.definition: An oral gift claim is not proved when the claimant’s accounts materially conflict and an available witness said to support the gift is not examined.

issues.legal_issue: A gift under Mahomedan law of property held by a trespasser is invalid if the donor neither delivers possession nor takes an overt step enabling the donee to obtain possession.
material_facts: The appellant claimed that the deceased made an oral gift of the property to him.
At the time of the alleged gift, the property was held by a person claiming adversely to the donor.
The donor neither delivered possession nor took any step to place the property within the appellant’s power to obtain possession.
The appellant did not obtain possession during the donor’s lifetime with the donor’s consent.
issues.conclusion: The alleged gift was invalid for want of delivery of possession or an overt act enabling the donee to obtain possession.
issues.legal_principle: A valid gift under Mahomedan law requires declaration, acceptance, and delivery of possession. Where the property is held by a trespasser, delivery may be replaced by an overt act by the donor that puts possession within the donee’s power to obtain; declaration and acceptance alone do not suffice. The Court relied on Mohammad Abdul Ghani v. Fakhr Jahan Begam, (1922) L.R. 49 I.A. 195; Mahomed Buksh Khan v. Hosseini Bibi, (1898) L.R. 15 I.A. 81; Mullic Abdool Guffoor v. Muleka, (1884) I.L.R. 10 Cal. 1112; and the cited rule in Hamilton’s Hedaya.

rule.if: muslim_gift_dispute and property_held_by_adverse_possessor and not possession_delivered and not donor_enabled_donee_to_obtain_possession

predicates.muslim_gift_dispute: A party claims property under a gift governed by Mahomedan law.
predicates.property_held_by_adverse_possessor: At the time of the alleged gift, another person holds the property while claiming adversely to the donor.
predicates.possession_delivered: The donor delivers possession of the property to the donee.
predicates.donor_enabled_donee_to_obtain_possession: The donor takes an overt step placing the property within the donee’s power to obtain possession.

issues.definition: A claimed gift is invalid when an adverse possessor holds the property and the donor neither delivers possession nor enables the donee to obtain it.

issues.legal_issue: An appeal is defective as to property when a necessary party’s death causes the appeal to abate against that party.
material_facts: During the appeal, an heir of a co-lessee in respect of one plot died.
The appeal abated against that heir.
The Court found the appeal defective for non-joinder as to that plot, but not as to the remaining property.
issues.conclusion: The appeal was defective for non-joinder as to the affected plot, but the defect did not extend to the rest of the appeal.
issues.legal_principle: The death and resulting abatement of a necessary party makes the appeal defective for non-joinder with respect to the property affected by that party’s interest; it does not necessarily defeat the appeal concerning other property.

rule.if: appeal_proceeding and necessary_party_died and appeal_abated_against_party and party_interest_limited_to_part_of_property

predicates.appeal_proceeding: A party brings an appeal concerning property.
predicates.necessary_party_died: A person whose presence is necessary to determine the appeal dies while it is pending.
predicates.appeal_abated_against_party: The appeal abates against the deceased person.
predicates.party_interest_limited_to_part_of_proper: The deceased person’s relevant interest concerns only part of the property in dispute.
predicates.appeal_defective_for_affected_property_o: The appeal is defective for non-joinder only as to the property affected by the deceased person’s interest.

issues.definition: When a necessary party dies, the appeal abates against that party, and that party’s interest concerns only part of the property, the appeal is defective only as to that part.
